candidates.text: Pull usage analytics for every feature and rank by percentage of active users who touch it in the last 90 days; cut anything below a hard threshold (e.g., under 2%).
Run a 'removal test' thought experiment: for each feature ask 'if this didn't exist today, would we build it now?' Cut anything the team answers 'no' to.
Calculate the engineering-hours-per-user-touch ratio for each feature and cut whichever has the worst maintenance cost relative to actual usage.
Hold a cross-functional 'star chamber' review where support, sales, design, and engineering each nominate three features they'd kill, and only features nominated by two or more groups get cut.
Conduct silent deprecation experiments: hide a feature behind a flag for a subset of users for two weeks and see if anyone notices or complains.
Audit support ticket volume per feature; anything generating disproportionate ticket load relative to its usage or revenue gets flagged for removal.
Use a zero-based feature budget: every feature must be re-justified from scratch each release cycle as if it were a brand-new proposal, or it's cut by default.
Ask engineers to independently estimate maintenance burden (hours/month) for each feature; rank and cut the highest-cost, lowest-value items first.
Run a blind card-sort exercise with real customers, asking them to sort features by importance; cut whatever consistently lands in the bottom quartile.
Interview a sample of recently churned customers specifically about what confused or overwhelmed them in the product, and cut features they mention as clutter.
Map every feature against the current strategic positioning statement; anything that no longer supports the stated strategy is a removal candidate regardless of usage.
Set a hard 'complexity budget' (e.g., max number of settings/screens) and force the team to cut enough features to fit under the cap before adding anything new.
Implement a one-in-one-out policy: no new feature ships without an existing one being removed in the same release.
Score each feature on a 2x2 matrix of 'usage' vs 'maintenance cost' and automatically cut anything in the low-usage/high-cost quadrant.
Have each team member privately rank all features from most to least valuable; aggregate the rankings and cut the bottom 10% by consensus score.
Analyze crash and bug reports by feature area; cut chronically buggy features that never get prioritized for fixing rather than continuing to patch them.
Look at revenue attribution: identify features not used by any paying customer segment and treat them as default removal candidates.
Run a pre-mortem workshop imagining the release failed because it was too cluttered, then work backward to identify which features likely caused the failure.
Check each feature's documentation and internal knowledge: if no one on the current team can explain how or why it works, treat that as a signal to cut it.
Survey internal support and sales staff on which features they actively avoid mentioning to customers because they're confusing or embarrassing.
Do a competitive teardown and identify features competitors have long since dropped; investigate whether keeping them still creates differentiation or just cost.
Track feature-flag toggle rates; if a configurable feature is disabled by the vast majority of accounts, consider removing it as the default or entirely.
Have design run a UI complexity audit measuring number of clicks, menu depth, and screen clutter, then cut whatever contributes most to cognitive load for the least benefit.
Segment usage by customer cohort (new vs. legacy) and identify features only legacy customers use; plan migration and removal instead of indefinite support.
Assess dependency risk: identify features built on deprecated, unsupported, or soon-to-be-unlicensed third-party components and cut those first.
Run an A/B test removing a feature for a subset of users and measure whether retention, satisfaction, or conversion actually changes.
Ask the exec team to imagine explaining the product to a new hire in five minutes; anything too obscure to mention in that pitch becomes a cut candidate.
Use session recordings to identify features that are frequently opened accidentally or immediately backed out of, signaling confusion rather than value.
Conduct a 'feature funeral' ritual each release cycle where the team nominates candidates for removal and publicly debates their merits before voting.
Calculate the ratio of support documentation pages to actual usage for each feature; disproportionately high documentation need relative to use signals removal.
Have the product team estimate opportunity cost: what could be built instead with the time spent maintaining each existing feature, and cut the worst-ROI ones.
Poll power users and 'super fans' specifically to identify which niche features they'd defend, then deliberately preserve those while cutting features nobody defends.
Track onboarding funnel drop-off points and identify features introduced during onboarding that correlate with higher abandonment, then simplify or remove them.
Perform a legal and compliance audit to identify features carrying disproportionate regulatory, privacy, or security risk relative to their benefit, and cut those.
Set an artificial release-day deadline forcing the team to strip the product down to only what's essential to ship, treating everything else as 'phase 2' or cut.
Analyze infrastructure and hosting costs per feature (compute, storage, API calls) and cut features that are disproportionately expensive to run given their usage.
Ask the customer advisory board directly: 'if we could only keep 80% of what exists today, what would you sacrifice?' and use their answers as a cut list.
Look for feature overlap or redundancy where two or more features solve the same problem in different ways, and consolidate by removing the weaker one.
Have engineering estimate the 'blast radius' of removing each feature (how many other systems depend on it) and prioritize cutting isolated, low-dependency features first.
Track how often a feature appears in release notes versus how often it appears in customer complaints, and cut anything with a poor investment-to-complaint ratio.
Use a regret-minimization framework: ask 'in one year, will we regret having kept this more than we'd regret cutting it?' for each borderline feature.
Analyze feature request volume from customers and identify existing features nobody has ever mentioned needing improved or has forgotten exist, then cut them.
Institute a rotating 'debt sprint' where engineers spend a week solely cataloguing unused code paths and dead features to bring cut candidates to product.
Bring in an outside consultant or fresh-eyes reviewer unfamiliar with the product to use it cold and flag anything confusing or seemingly unnecessary.
Cut based on staleness: any feature that hasn't received a meaningful update, bug fix, or usage spike in over a year is flagged as a default candidate.
Run an internal dogfooding audit: track which features the company's own employees never use in daily operation, treating internal neglect as an external usage proxy.
Have finance model the total cost of ownership for each feature (support, infra, QA, dev time) and rank cuts purely by highest TCO relative to revenue generated.
Use a 'time to value' analysis: cut features that take disproportionately long for a new user to discover or benefit from relative to their overall importance.
Ask each team to write a one-paragraph justification for why their favorite feature should stay; cut anything for which no one can produce a compelling paragraph.
Analyze test coverage and QA effort per feature; cut features that consume excessive QA cycles each release without corresponding business value.
Track accessibility and localization burden per feature; deprioritize niche features that require disproportionate investment to support across languages or devices.
Use a lightweight RICE-style scoring (reach, impact, confidence, effort) in reverse to score existing features, then cut those scoring lowest for continued investment.
Set up a customer-facing 'vote to keep' campaign for borderline features, publicly showing usage stats and letting the community decide via engagement.
Have leadership define three non-negotiable 'north star' use cases for the release, then cut any feature that doesn't directly serve one of them.
Look at feature adoption decay curves over time (not just current usage) to identify features that were popular at launch but have been steadily abandoned.
Cross-reference features against known upcoming platform or OS changes, and cut anything that will soon become incompatible or unsupported anyway.
Run a 'silent stakeholder' exercise where someone plays devil's advocate for total simplicity, arguing to cut every feature unless another team member actively defends it.

candidates.text: Usage telemetry audit: rank every feature by active-user percentage over the last 90 days and cut anything below a set threshold.
Support-ticket cost analysis: identify features generating disproportionate support burden relative to usage and cut the worst offenders.
Zero-based feature budgeting: require every feature to be re-justified from scratch as if it didn't exist, rather than assuming it stays by default.
Engineering maintenance tax survey: ask engineers to score each feature by how much ongoing complexity/tech debt it imposes, then cut the highest-cost, lowest-value ones.
Customer willingness-to-pay test: survey or A/B test whether removing a feature changes conversion or churn; cut features nobody would miss enough to pay for.
Strategic alignment filter: map every feature against the current company strategy/north star and remove anything that no longer serves it, regardless of usage.
Kill-switch experiment: silently disable a feature for a subset of users for two weeks and measure complaint volume and behavior change before deciding permanently.
Cognitive load audit: have a UX researcher walk through the product noting every extra decision point or menu item, then cut ones that add friction without clear benefit.
Competitive differentiation check: cut anything that's purely at-parity with competitors and doesn't contribute to a unique value proposition.
Revenue attribution modeling: run each feature through an attribution model to see which are actually correlated with revenue-generating behavior, deprioritizing the rest.
Support team veto power: let frontline support and success teams nominate the three features causing the most confusion or complaints for removal.
Sunset by cohort: identify features only used by legacy/grandfathered customer segments and phase them out as those segments shrink.
Red team the roadmap: assign a small group to argue for deletion of each planned feature as if they were a hostile critic, and weigh their strongest arguments.
Time-to-value scoring: measure how long it takes new users to reach value with vs without each feature in their path; cut ones that measurably slow onboarding.
Code coverage/test debt lens: cut features with the least test coverage and highest bug rates as a proxy for hidden risk and cost.
Executive one-pager forcing function: require any feature staying in the release to have a one-page business case; anything without one is automatically cut.
External advisory panel: bring in 3-5 non-employee power users to review the product live and flag what feels bloated or unnecessary.
Feature entropy ranking: use analytics to find features with declining usage trendlines (not just low usage) and cut those on a downward trajectory.
Support cost vs. revenue ratio: calculate literal dollar cost of maintaining/supporting a feature against dollar revenue it drives, cut negative-ROI items.
Design system consistency review: remove UI patterns/features that violate the current design system or introduce one-off patterns needing special handling.
Founder gut-check veto: have the founder/CEO personally review the release and unilaterally strike anything that doesn't feel core to the product vision.
Customer journey mapping deletion pass: walk the full journey and remove any touchpoint that doesn't clearly move the user toward activation, retention, or expansion.
Blind ranking exercise: have each team member independently rank all features by importance without discussion, then cut anything that ranks in the bottom quartile across raters.
Data-instrumentation gap rule: if a feature isn't instrumented well enough to prove its value, treat that as grounds for removal pending proper measurement.
Legal/compliance risk sweep: cut features that create outsized regulatory, privacy, or security exposure relative to their benefit.
Reverse roadmap workshop: run a workshop where the only agenda is generating a removal list, treating deletion ideas with the same rigor as feature ideas.
Load-bearing wall test: for each feature, ask 'if we removed this, what breaks downstream?' and cut anything with no dependencies and low direct usage.
Onboarding funnel drop-off analysis: identify steps or features correlated with user drop-off and cut or simplify the biggest offenders.
Naming and surface area audit: count total menu items, settings, and screens; set a hard cap on surface area and force trade-off decisions to fit under it.
Customer interview 'would you notice' test: directly ask a sample of customers to guess which features exist; anything nobody can recall using becomes a removal candidate.

candidates.text: Flat single-price subscription: one price, one tier, no add-ons -- everyone pays the same amount regardless of usage or company size, maximizing simplicity and removing decision paralysis at signup.
Good/Better/Best three-tier ladder (e.g., Basic, Pro, Enterprise) with a deliberately weaker 'decoy' middle tier engineered to nudge most buyers toward the higher-margin option.
Usage-based metered pricing that charges per unit consumed (e.g., per API call, per document, per GB), so cost scales directly with value received and is billed monthly in arrears.
Per-seat/per-user licensing with volume discounts that kick in automatically once a customer's team crosses defined headcount thresholds.
Freemium model: a genuinely useful free tier forever, with paid upgrades unlocked only once usage crosses a threshold or advanced features are needed, funding growth through viral adoption.
Value-based pricing set as a percentage of the quantifiable outcome delivered (e.g., cost saved, revenue generated, hours reclaimed) rather than tied to the cost of delivering the service.
Reverse/opt-down trial: give new signups full premium access for a limited period, then auto-downgrade them to a lower or free tier unless they actively choose to pay, leveraging loss aversion.
Founding-member charter pricing: lock in a steep, permanent discount for the first N customers who join during a pre-launch window, to seed early traction and word-of-mouth.
Penetration pricing: launch well below perceived market value to capture share quickly, with planned, telegraphed price increases in later phases once switching costs and a user base exist.
Price-skimming: launch at a premium aimed at early adopters and prestige-seekers, then step the price down over time as the market matures and competitors appear.
Pay-what-you-want pricing with a suggested anchor and a hard minimum floor, relying on trust and reciprocity norms to keep average revenue viable.
Prepaid credits/token wallet: customers buy a pool of credits upfront that different features consume at different rates, decoupling billing from a rigid monthly subscription cycle.
Monthly-vs-annual discount ladder: identical tiers priced both ways, with a meaningful (~15-20%) discount for annual prepayment to improve cash flow and reduce churn.
Geographic/PPP-adjusted pricing that varies the sticker price by country based on local purchasing power, expanding the addressable market internationally instead of using one-size-fits-all pricing.
Two-track enterprise model: transparent self-serve pricing for individuals and small teams, paired with a 'contact sales' negotiated-quote track for larger organizations needing custom terms.
Van Westendorp price-sensitivity survey run with target customers pre-launch (too cheap / cheap / expensive / too expensive) to mathematically identify the optimal price point before committing.
Conjoint-analysis-driven bundling: use structured trade-off studies to learn which features customers actually value, then build tier contents and prices around that data rather than intuition.

Cost-plus pricing: calculate the fully loaded cost to serve one customer (infrastructure, support, payment fees) and add a fixed target margin, guaranteeing profitability independent of market benchmarks.
Competitor-anchored pricing that sets the price at parity with, or a small percentage below, the dominant competitor's equivalent tier, competing on brand and features instead of price.
Outcome-only/results-based pricing: charge nothing, or only a small platform fee, unless the product produces a pre-agreed measurable result, shifting commercial risk from buyer to seller.
Risk-reversal overlay: keep whatever core pricing model is chosen, but wrap it in an unconditional 30-, 60-, or 90-day money-back guarantee to lower the psychological barrier to purchase.

Dynamic, personalized pricing algorithm that varies the price shown to different visitors in real time based on signals like referral source, device, or stated willingness-to-pay, continuously optimized.
Hybrid base-plus-overage pricing: a flat monthly fee includes a set usage allowance, with metered overage charges billed only for consumption beyond that included amount.
Family/group plan bundling: one subscription covers multiple individual seats or profiles at a per-unit discount versus buying separately, targeting households or small teams.
Permanent nonprofit/education/startup discount tier, clearly published (e.g., 50% off) for verified students, registered nonprofits, or pre-revenue startups.
Sponsored-seat / pay-it-forward model where paying customers or partner organizations can fund subscriptions for others, creating a two-sided revenue structure alongside direct payment.
Pre-launch bidding/auction for a capacity-constrained beta cohort, letting prospective customers reveal true willingness-to-pay while generating early revenue and buzz.
Modular a la carte pricing: unbundle the product into separately priced add-on features so customers assemble and pay only for the specific capabilities they need.
Grandfathered legacy pricing: publicly commit that existing subscribers keep their sign-up price forever even as list price rises for new customers, rewarding loyalty and de-risking future increases.
Barter/non-cash pricing: let qualifying users pay via promotion, user-generated content, referrals, or data-sharing agreements instead of, or alongside, a cash subscription fee.

candidates.text: Grandfather all current customers at their existing price for a set transition period (e.g., 6-12 months) while new sign-ups pay the higher price immediately, reducing backlash from your most loyal base.

Introduce a new premium tier at the higher price and keep a limited-feature legacy tier at the old price, letting price-sensitive customers self-select downward instead of leaving entirely.

Offer a 'price lock' for customers who commit to a longer contract or annual prepayment, turning the increase into a loyalty incentive rather than a penalty.
Quietly reduce package size, portion, or included quota while holding the sticker price constant (shrinkflation), raising effective price without a visible number change.
Unbundle features or services that were previously included and charge separately for them, effectively raising average revenue per customer without changing the headline price.
Use anchor pricing: show a higher 'reference' price crossed out next to the new price, framing the increase as a discount off a higher value rather than a hike.
Time the announcement to coincide with a well-publicized external cost driver (inflation, raw materials, tariffs, energy costs), giving customers an easily accepted, non-company-specific rationale.
Pilot the new price in a limited region, channel, or customer segment first, measure churn and revenue impact, then adjust before a full rollout.
Pair the increase with a stronger guarantee (extended money-back window, price-match promise, satisfaction guarantee) to reduce the perceived risk of paying more.
Apply the new price primarily at natural renewal or re-enrollment moments, when switching friction and customer attention are both lower than at an arbitrary announcement date.
Convert the offering into a tiered membership or subscription model with added perks (exclusive content, priority service, community access) that justify a higher recurring price.
Introduce installment or financing options so the higher total cost is broken into smaller periodic payments that feel more affordable.
Reframe the price in small daily/per-use terms ('just $1.30/day') instead of the total period cost, shrinking the perceived size of the increase.
Repackage and reposition the brand as a premium option — upgraded packaging, service experience, and marketing — so the higher price aligns with a clearly upgraded perception.
Let customers opt into the new pricing early in exchange for a bonus (extra credit, bonus product, early-access feature), turning the increase into a choice rather than an imposition.
Launch or expand a loyalty/rewards program (points, cashback, exclusive perks) timed with the price change so repeat customers feel compensated for paying more.
Raise prices selectively on the least price-sensitive products or segments first, leaving flagship or highly visible items untouched to protect brand perception.
Introduce a stripped-down 'lite' or 'classic' version at the old price point for budget-conscious customers, while the main product moves to the new higher price.
Use dynamic or personalized pricing algorithms that adjust based on each customer's individual willingness to pay, rather than applying one uniform increase to everyone.
Publish a transparent breakdown of costs (materials, labor, sustainability investments) showing customers exactly why prices are rising, building trust through openness.
Frame part of the increase as funding a cause (sustainability initiative, charitable donation, ethical sourcing) so customers associate the higher price with a value they care about.
Give existing customers a one-time transition credit or voucher that softens the first billing cycle at the new price, while the increase remains permanent going forward.
Raise ancillary charges (shipping, service fees, handling) rather than the core listed price, keeping the advertised price point stable and only the total checkout cost higher.
Launch a new/upgraded product version at the higher price and gradually phase out the old version, framing the change as an upgrade path rather than a straight price hike.
Build automatic annual escalation clauses into new contracts upfront (e.g., 3% per year), so future increases are pre-agreed and expected rather than a surprise renegotiation.
Add a very high-priced 'ultra-premium' tier alongside the new standard price, using the decoy effect to make the actual increase look modest and reasonable by comparison.

candidates.text: Phase the increase in gradually through several small steps over 12-18 months rather than one large jump, so no single change feels shocking.
Pair the price rise with a visible upgrade—new features, better materials, extended warranty—launched simultaneously so customers see 'more' alongside 'costs more'.
Grandfather existing subscribers at their current rate for a defined transition period while new customers pay the higher price immediately.
Introduce a lower-cost 'lite' or stripped-down tier alongside the higher-priced standard plan, giving budget-conscious customers a way to stay rather than leave entirely.
Add the increase as a separate itemized fee (e.g., a 'service' or 'sustainability' charge) instead of raising the visible headline price.
Proactively and transparently explain the specific cost drivers behind the increase (labor, materials, energy) rather than announcing it without context.
Frame the increase explicitly as a pass-through of external pressures—supplier costs, tariffs, currency shifts—positioning the company as reluctant, not opportunistic.
Give customers 60-90 days' advance notice so they can plan and budget, reducing the sense of being ambushed.
Offer a limited 'lock in now' window letting customers pre-pay, renew early, or extend contracts at the old price before the new one takes effect.
Launch a premium tier priced well above the new standard rate so the standard increase looks modest by comparison (price anchoring).
Add a deliberately unattractive middle-priced 'decoy' option that steers customers toward a higher-margin plan they now perceive as the better deal.
Shift from flat-rate to usage-based or metered pricing so light users see little or no change while heavier users absorb most of the increase.
Use customer data to personalize the increase, raising prices more for low price-sensitivity segments and less (or not at all) for customers flagged as high churn risk.
Bundle the product with complementary services or add-ons so the per-item price increase is offset by added perceived value in the package.
Create a loyalty or 'founding member' program that locks in discounted pricing for long-tenured customers as a reward for staying.
Offer a one-time credit, bonus, or loyalty points balance that offsets part of the increase during the first billing cycle after the change.
Time the price change announcement to coincide with a contract renewal or annual cycle customers already expect, rather than mid-term.
Simultaneously remove a friction point elsewhere (waive a fee, ease the return policy, add a small free perk) so the overall change feels net-neutral or positive.
Pilot the new price in one market, channel, or segment first, then refine the amount and messaging based on observed churn before rolling it out broadly.
Quietly reduce package size, included units, or service scope while holding the sticker price constant, effectively raising the per-unit price without a visible number change.
Reposition the brand as premium through improved packaging, service experience, and marketing so the higher price matches an upgraded perceived quality tier.
Build automatic, pre-disclosed escalator clauses into new contracts (e.g., annual inflation-linked increases) so future hikes are expected rather than sudden.
Give customers an explicit choice at renewal: accept the new price or downgrade to a reduced feature set at the old price, keeping them in the ecosystem either way.
Move to dynamic, demand-based pricing so increases concentrate in peak-demand periods and stay less visible during off-peak times.
Accept the loss of the least profitable, highest-cost-to-serve customer segment on purpose, letting the increase act as a natural filter while retaining higher-value customers.
Introduce an optional membership or subscription upgrade that bundles the higher price with added perks, framing it as a choice rather than an imposed hike.
Survey or convene a panel of loyal customers before finalizing the change, incorporating their feedback so they feel ownership of the decision when it's announced.
Tie part of the increase to a cause customers value (e.g., 'this portion funds our recycling program'), giving them a value-aligned reason to accept paying more.
Offer a temporary price-protection or match guarantee after the increase, reducing the risk customers feel in staying rather than shopping around.
Roll the increase out first in geographies or channels with historically lower price sensitivity, then extend it company-wide once validated.

candidates.text: One-click "Export current view" button on every table/list that downloads exactly what's on screen (respecting active filters and sort order) as CSV or Excel.
Scheduled recurring exports: users configure a report to auto-generate daily, weekly, or monthly and be delivered automatically without any manual trigger.
A destination picker at export time: instead of only "download," let users choose where each export goes — email attachment, Slack channel, Google Drive, Dropbox, or SFTP — from a simple dropdown.
Full-account data portability export: a single button bundles the user's entire dataset into a self-contained archive (JSON/CSV plus documentation) for backup, migration, or GDPR-style data requests.
A drag-and-drop report/template builder where users design a branded, formatted layout (logo, headers, field order) once and reuse it to generate polished PDF exports repeatedly.
API-first export with no dedicated UI: publish a documented REST or GraphQL endpoint so developers pull exactly the data they need programmatically, on whatever cadence they choose.
An in-app command syntax where power users type structured commands like `export table=orders format=json filter="status:open"` to trigger exports without navigating menus.
Contextual selection export: users check specific rows or cells and export just that ad hoc subset, independent of any saved view or filter.
Delta/incremental export mode: the system remembers each user's last export and offers "export changes since last time" to support lightweight ongoing syncing with external tools.
Background job export with resumable download: large exports run asynchronously in chunks and produce a link the user can return to later to resume or retry.
Natural-language export requests through a chat-style assistant: the user types "give me last quarter's top customers as a PDF" and the system parses it into filters and format automatically.
A live shareable link export that generates a read-only web page URL always reflecting current data, optionally with an expiration date or password protection, instead of a static file.
Embeddable export: produce an iframe or script snippet so an exported chart or table can be pasted into an external website or wiki and continue updating live.
A print-first export mode: a dedicated preview that mirrors exact on-screen styling with page breaks, headers, footers, and page numbers, aimed at handing physical or emailed reports to stakeholders.
Prebuilt integration connectors that treat "export" as a sync action into another tool, e.g., one-click push to Salesforce, HubSpot, Notion, or Google Sheets.
Continuous data-warehouse replication for analytics teams: a managed pipeline that streams data continuously into Snowflake, BigQuery, or Redshift instead of producing discrete export files.
A round-trip export format that preserves internal IDs and relationships so the exported file can later be re-imported to restore, clone, or migrate the exact dataset.
Async notify-when-ready export: the user requests an export and keeps working, then gets an email or in-app notification with a secure download link once the job finishes.
Saved export presets: users name and store specific field/filter/format combinations as reusable "recipes" they or teammates can re-run with a single click.
Admin-governed export policy: organization admins define who can export which data, require approval workflows for sensitive datasets, and review an audit log of every export event.
A multi-format bundle export where one action produces a single zip containing the same data simultaneously as CSV, JSON, and a summary PDF for different downstream needs.
A copy-to-clipboard micro-export: a lightweight "Copy as Markdown/CSV" action that puts formatted data on the clipboard instantly for pasting into chat or docs, skipping files entirely.
An anonymized/redacted export mode with a toggle that automatically masks or strips PII and sensitive fields, intended for data shared externally or with analytics vendors.
Custom transform scripting: a small sandboxed scripting hook (like a JS function) letting advanced users reshape, rename, or calculate fields during the export process itself.
Chatbot-triggered export: typing a slash command such as `/export weekly-report` inside Slack or Teams generates the file and posts it directly into that conversation.
A visual snapshot export that captures the current screen as a static image (PNG/SVG), suited to dashboards and charts where visual fidelity matters more than raw numbers.
Tiered export capability: basic CSV export is free for everyone, while scheduling, branding, advanced formats, and API access are reserved for paid plans.
Voice-assistant export: integration with Alexa, Google Assistant, or Siri so a spoken request like "export today's sales report" triggers generation and delivery by email.
An offline-ready export package: a self-contained static HTML bundle or QR-code link that works without internet access, useful for field teams or air-gapped environments.
A live document push export that writes data directly into an editable, shareable Google Sheet or Notion database the user owns, rather than producing a static downloadable file.

candidates.text: Pull product analytics data and set a hard usage-frequency threshold (say, fewer than 2% of active users touching it per month); anything below the line becomes an automatic removal candidate pending a sanity check.

Instead of looking at absolute usage, plot each feature's usage trend over the last 12-18 months and prioritize cutting features in steady decline, since a shrinking feature is a truer signal of fading relevance than one that's small but stable.

Cluster features by the underlying user need they serve rather than by name, and when two or more overlap, cut whichever one is used less or costs more to maintain, treating internal redundancy itself as a removal criterion.
Attach a real cost figure to each feature (cloud spend, third-party API fees, support hours, QA time) and remove anything whose carrying cost clearly outweighs the value it demonstrably returns.

Build a rough profit-and-loss statement per feature (attributable revenue or retention impact minus build-and-maintenance cost) and cut from the bottom of the ranked list until the release feels lean enough.

Reframe every 'should we keep this' question as 'what else could this team build with the hours this feature costs annually,' and let comparative future value decide the cut rather than the feature's merit in isolation.

Audit every paid third-party library, API, or vendor contract embedded in the product, and flag features that exist mainly to justify an expensive or soon-renewing dependency as prime candidates for removal.

Mine the last two quarters of support tickets, tag them by feature, and cut whichever features generate a disproportionate volume of confusion or complaints relative to how many people actually use them.

Read through churn-survey verbatims and cancellation interviews specifically hunting for features described as clutter or confusing, and let recurring real-world complaints outrank internal opinion about what matters.

Run static analysis or an AI-assisted code review across the codebase to surface orphaned modules with no recent commits, no incoming calls, or no linked analytics events, then confirm and cut whatever nobody can explain.

Score features by the technical debt and coupling they introduce (how many other changes they block, how often they cause regressions elsewhere) and remove whichever has the worst debt-to-value ratio even if its usage looks healthy.

Print every screen and feature on a card, pin them to a wall, and let a cross-functional group place a limited number of dot stickers on what they'd protect; whatever draws zero dots is fair game to cut.

Give each stakeholder a fixed pot of fake currency and run an auction where they bid to keep features; whatever goes unbid or draws only token bids surfaces as a consensus-backed cut without anyone having to publicly nominate it.

Have each team member privately draft a personal cut list before any group discussion, then compare lists for overlap; items several people flagged independently carry far more weight than one strong opinion voiced in a meeting.

Appoint a rotating devil's advocate whose explicit job is to argue for cutting every feature under discussion; anything that survives their attack with a genuinely strong counter-argument stays, everything else goes.

Give a sample of real customers a card-sorting exercise across the full feature list, sorting each into essential, nice-to-have, or didn't-know-this-existed, and cut whatever clusters reliably into the bottom bucket.

For each feature under review, trace who originally requested it and why; if that person has left, changed roles, or stopped caring, treat the feature as having lost its last line of defense and prioritize it for removal.

Adopt a standing one-in-one-out rule: no new feature ships without an existing feature of comparable footprint being retired in the same release, forcing the trade-off to happen every cycle instead of never.

Ship every new or experimental feature with a pre-committed sunset date and explicit success bar set at launch, so removing it later is a scheduled default rather than a fresh, politically fraught debate.

Run a zero-based budgeting exercise for features: every one starts the cycle at zero, and its owner must actively re-justify its continued existence with current data or it is automatically slated for removal.

Rank every feature by the security exposure, privacy liability, or regulatory burden it adds, and cut any whose risk footprint is clearly out of proportion to its actual usage or revenue contribution.

Cross-reference every removal candidate against active enterprise contracts and service-level agreements to filter out anything contractually protected, then apply your cutting criteria only to what remains.

Classify every candidate cut by how reversible it would be (a flag flip versus a data-migration-requiring teardown) and knock out the easy, low-risk items first while queuing the irreversible ones for deeper review.

Have one senior leader with full cross-functional context simply make the call directly, on the logic that speed and decisiveness matter more here than consensus, accepting an occasional wrong call as the price of momentum.

Look at which customer segments or use cases the company has explicitly decided to deprioritize strategically, and cut the features that exist mainly to serve those segments even if their raw usage numbers still look respectable.

Do a teardown of two or three leading competitors' current products and flag anything your product has that none of them bother building, using that absence as a prompt to question why you still carry it.

Quietly disable a suspected low-value feature behind a flag for a subset of users without announcing it, then measure whether support volume, churn, or engagement actually move before deciding whether to cut it for everyone.

Sweep the product for orphaned features with no current owner, no one on the team who fully understands them, or no documentation, and treat that orphan status itself as a signal to remove.

3. ShowerCaddyPro: A quick-drain mesh shower caddy with a rotating hook system that hangs on communal dorm shower rails, keeping shampoo and soap off wet floors and easy to grab-and-go to shared bathrooms. Retail under $18.

4. NoiseBuds Foam Kit: A pack of reusable silicone earplugs plus a small carrying case, marketed for studying in noisy dorms or sleeping through loud roommates, with three fit sizes included. Sold under $10 at campus stores.

5. StackCrate: A collapsible plastic storage crate that folds flat for move-in day and pops up into a sturdy under-bed bin, sized to fit standard dorm bed heights, useful for off-season clothes or shoes. Priced at $25.

6. MicroFridge Organizer Bins: A set of stackable, clear plastic bins sized precisely for mini dorm fridges, letting students separate snacks, drinks, and leftovers so nothing gets lost in the back. Sold as a 3-pack under $15.

7. WhiteboardPlanner: A magnetic dry-erase weekly planner sized to stick on the inside of a dorm closet door, with a marker holder and pre-printed class/assignment columns, replacing paper planners that get lost. Priced under $12.

8. CableCorral: A silicone cable organizer tray that sits on a desk holding chargers, mice, and earbuds in labeled slots, preventing the tangled charger drawer problem common in shared rooms. Sold under $10.

9. LaundryHaulBag: A heavy-duty, wheeled laundry bag with a drawstring top and reinforced base, designed for hauling clothes across campus to communal laundry rooms without needing a full hamper set. Priced around $22.

10. PortableClothesRack: A collapsible aluminum clothes rack that assembles without tools, fitting inside dorm closets that lack enough hanging space, folding down to slide under a bed when not needed. Retail $30.

11. StudySnackBox: A reusable divided silicone snack container with airtight lids, designed for carrying study session snacks to the library without crumbs or spills, dishwasher safe and collapsible for storage. Priced under $12.

12. PillowSpeaker Wrap: A thin flat speaker pad that slips inside a pillowcase and connects via Bluetooth, letting students listen to music or podcasts while falling asleep without disturbing roommates with earbuds. Priced at $28.

13. GripStudyStand: An adjustable, foldable aluminum stand for holding textbooks, laptops, or tablets at eye level on a dorm desk, reducing neck strain during long study sessions and folding flat for backpacks. Priced $18.

14. HighlighterGripSet: An ergonomic set of six highlighters with wide rubberized grips designed for long annotation sessions, packaged with a slim case that clips onto a binder ring for easy carry. Under $10.

15. DormDoorMirror: A shatterproof full-length mirror with adhesive-strip mounting designed to attach to the back of a standard dorm door without drilling, including a small shelf for accessories at the bottom edge. Priced at $20.

16. PowerStripTower: A vertical surge-protected power strip with USB-A and USB-C ports stacked on a small footprint base, designed for dorm rooms where outlets are scarce and desks are crowded with electronics. Retail $25.

17. InstantOatmealTumbler: A double-walled tumbler with a built-in mesh strainer insert, letting students make instant oatmeal or overnight oats directly in the cup for breakfast on the way to class. Priced under $18.

18. FoldFlatHamper: A pop-up mesh laundry hamper that collapses to less than an inch thick for storage under a bed, with reinforced handles for carrying to laundry rooms, sold in bright colors. Priced $14.

19. BackpackRainShell: A lightweight, packable waterproof cover that stretches over any standard backpack, protecting laptops and books during sudden rain while walking between classes, folding into its own zip pouch. Priced under $15.

20. StudyPostureCushion: A memory foam lumbar cushion with an elastic strap designed to attach to standard dorm desk chairs, improving posture during marathon study sessions without needing a chair replacement. Priced $22.
21. MicrowaveMugSet: A set of two silicone collapsible mugs safe for microwave use, designed for making ramen, mac and cheese, or tea in a dorm room without needing bowls or pots. Priced under $16.
22. ClipOnFanLight: A small USB-powered clip fan with an attached LED light ring, designed to clamp onto a dorm desk or bed frame for airflow and light in rooms without ceiling fans. Priced $20.

23. ExamDayKit: A small zip pouch pre-packed with two pencils, an eraser, a mini calculator, and earplugs, marketed as a grab-and-go essential for test days sold at campus bookstores. Priced under $12.

24. UnderDeskBikeStorage Hook: A wall-mounted folding hook rated for bike frames, designed to let students store bikes vertically in small dorm rooms or shared apartment hallways, installed with adhesive or screws. Priced $25.

25. ReusableToGoContainer Stack: A set of three stackable, leak-proof containers with snap lids sized for dining hall to-go meals, designed to reduce disposable container waste and fit in backpacks. Priced under $20.

26. DormRoomTapeLightKit: A peel-and-stick LED strip light kit with a remote for color and brightness, designed for renters who can't paint walls but want ambient lighting, easily removable without damage. Priced $28.

27. StudyTimerBlock: A physical wooden cube timer with preset study/break intervals marked on each face, flip to start a session, designed as a screen-free alternative to phone timers for focus. Priced under $18.
28. CompactIroningMat: A heat-resistant, foldable ironing mat that rolls up small enough for a dorm drawer, used directly on a bed or desk since most dorms lack ironing boards. Priced $15.

29. GroceryTote Cart: A foldable two-wheeled utility cart with a removable canvas tote, designed for students without cars to haul groceries or laundry across campus, collapsing flat for closet storage. Priced $35.

30. NightGuardMouthTray Kit: A basic boil-and-bite mouthguard kit marketed for stressed students who grind their teeth during exam season, packaged with a travel case and simple instructions. Priced under $15.

candidates.text: Pull 90-day usage analytics for every feature and cut anything in the bottom decile of active usage, weighted by segment value.
Build a maintenance cost ledger: have engineers log hours spent fixing/supporting each feature over the last quarter, then rank and cut the highest-cost/lowest-value items.
Run an inverted RICE score: instead of prioritizing new work, score existing features on reach and impact versus ongoing effort, and cut the low-reach/high-effort tail.
Do a 'would we build this today' vote: walk the team through each existing feature as if it were a fresh proposal and cut anything that doesn't get a majority yes.
Interview 5-8 heavy users and ask what they never touch; anything nobody mentions using becomes a candidate cut list.
Map feature dependencies into a graph and identify orphaned modules with no downstream reliance -- these are safe, low-risk cuts.
Silently disable a handful of low-confidence features behind a flag for one week and measure complaint/support volume as a real-world cut signal.
Attribute revenue and retention impact to each feature via funnel/cohort analysis, and cut anything with zero measurable business contribution.
Audit any feature launched with an explicit success metric or sunset clause and enforce the original criteria -- if it never hit its target, cut it now.
Open a 'cut proposal' doc where anyone can submit a one-page case for removing something; review and decide in a single weekly meeting.
Run a static-analysis heatmap of code complexity and change frequency; flag high-churn, high-complexity modules as prime removal candidates regardless of feature popularity.
Calculate support cost per feature by dividing support ticket hours by monthly active users, and cut the highest-cost-per-user offenders.
List every current feature against the company's current strategic pillars/OKRs and cut anything that doesn't map to a pillar.
Hold a timeboxed team brainstorm where every member nominates their top 3 things to cut, then tally votes to build a ranked shortlist.
Dedicate one full sprint explicitly to removal work, scoping it from the combined nominations of the whole team rather than new feature work.
Announce a planned deprecation publicly before committing, and use the volume/intensity of user pushback as the real decision signal.
Compare the engineering hours saved per quarter by removing a feature against the one-time cost of removing it, and only cut when the payback period is short.
Run a security/compliance audit of dependencies and flag any feature relying on outdated or vulnerable libraries as a priority cut over feature value.
Identify redundant features that solve the same problem two different ways, and cut whichever path has lower usage or adoption.
Build a customer segment impact matrix mapping features to which paying segments use them, and cut anything serving less than a defined minimum share of revenue-bearing customers.
Audit admin-only toggles, legacy settings, and internal flags for zero engagement over the last year as easy, low-controversy cuts.
Analyze onboarding funnel drop-off points and cut or simplify any UI step correlated with the highest abandonment rate.
Flag any feature whose documentation hasn't been updated in two or more release cycles as a signal of abandonment, then formally review it for removal.
Do a quick competitor scan and cut any feature that's neither differentiating nor table-stakes compared to what competitors ship.
Review support macros/canned responses; if multiple exist just to explain workarounds for a feature, treat that as a strong cut signal.
Ask each engineer individually, 'If you left tomorrow, what would nobody be able to support?' and use the answers to flag either investment or removal targets.
Audit app bundle size and load-time budget contributions per feature, and cut or defer whichever features disproportionately hurt performance for their usage level.
Do a post-mortem on the last 3-4 releases' new features, checking current usage data, and cut anything that never gained real traction after launch.
Run a mock 'budget cut' exercise with leadership where they must hypothetically remove 20% of scope, then cross-reference their picks with engineering effort data for a sanity-checked cut list.
Set a hard rule that for every new feature shipped this release, one existing feature of comparable maintenance cost must be identified for removal.
Survey customer success/sales teams for the features they most often have to explain away or apologize for, and treat repeated mentions as cut candidates.

agents.stance: PRAGMATIST: practical, resource-aware, shippable. Favor ideas that a small team could start on Monday. Prefer clarity and feasibility over cleverness.

candidates.text: Pull usage analytics for every feature over the last 90 days and set a hard threshold (e.g., <2% of active users); anything below it goes on the cut list by default unless someone argues it's strategically necessary.
Cross-reference support ticket volume against usage data to find features that consume disproportionate support time relative to how many people actually use them, and cut those first.
Have engineering log actual maintenance hours (bug fixes, on-call pages, code review) per feature over the last quarter; rank by cost and cut the highest-cost, lowest-value items.
Run a two-week feature-flag kill switch on a low-confidence feature for a subset of users and measure complaint volume and metric shifts before deciding to remove it permanently.
Interview the ten most engaged customers and directly ask which features they'd be fine losing tomorrow; use their answers as a sanity check against internal assumptions.
Map every feature to a revenue or retention metric; anything with no measurable link to either becomes a cut candidate.
Have each team member privately submit their top three 'features I'd cut' with one sentence of rationale, then tally overlaps as the starting cut list.
Re-pitch every existing feature to leadership as if it were a brand-new proposal; if it wouldn't get greenlit today, it's a candidate for removal.
Build a simple 2x2 matrix (maintenance effort vs. strategic value) and plot every feature on it; cut everything landing in the high-effort/low-value quadrant.
Track how often support macros or FAQ articles for a given feature get used relative to the feature's actual usage; high lookup rate with low usage signals a confusing, cuttable feature.
Post a public deprecation notice for a shortlist of features and measure the volume and specificity of pushback as a real-world signal of actual value versus assumed value.
Have engineering flag features tied to the most fragile, poorly-tested, or legacy code paths; prioritize cutting these to reduce release risk even if usage is moderate.
Review onboarding funnel drop-off data and identify any features that create friction or confusion for new users; cut or hide those regardless of overall usage.
Dedicate one full-day 'cutting sprint' where the whole team reviews the current feature list against this quarter's stated goals and votes to remove anything not clearly serving them.
Compare your feature set to your top two competitors' and identify features that exist purely for parity but drive no differentiation or usage; cut those first.
Plot usage trend lines (not just snapshots) for every feature over 6-12 months; cut anything showing sustained decline even if current absolute usage looks okay.
Map every feature to the user personas it serves; where two or more features serve the same persona and job-to-be-done, cut the weaker overlapping one.
Calculate support cost per active user for each feature and cut the ones with the worst ratio, since they're taxing the team out of proportion to their value.
Run a cross-functional 'kill list' workshop with support, sales, design, and engineering each nominating features with written rationale, then score nominations as a group.
Have engineering map feature dependencies and identify the ones with the fewest downstream integrations or dependents; these are the lowest-risk, easiest cuts to start with.
Have legal/security flag any features creating outsized compliance, privacy, or security exposure relative to their usage or value, and prioritize those for removal.
Audit every feature still sitting behind an experimental or beta flag that never graduated to general availability; default-remove anything that's been dormant there for 6+ months.
Have the PM, engineering lead, and support lead independently score every feature 1-5 on value and cost, then compare scores and investigate any big discrepancies before finalizing cuts.
Send a short 'why did you stop using this' survey to users who abandoned a specific feature, using their responses to confirm or reject a cut decision.
A/B test removal: hide a feature for a control group of users for two weeks and measure retention, conversion, or satisfaction metrics before deciding to remove it for everyone.
Audit documentation and training material volume per feature; features requiring disproportionate docs relative to usage are flagged as complexity worth removing.
Score every existing feature against your current strategic pillars/roadmap themes on a simple scale; anything scoring zero alignment gets cut regardless of how much was invested in it originally.
Explicitly write down the sunk cost (time, money) already spent on each feature, then deliberately set that number aside and decide purely based on future value and cost to keep.
Tag cloud/infrastructure costs by feature and identify which features consume disproportionate server spend relative to their usage or revenue contribution; cut the worst offenders.
Quietly remove a feature for a small percentage of users without announcement and monitor churn, support contacts, and engagement for two weeks as a low-noise real-world test.

candidates.text: Develop a low-cost smartphone app using leaf-image classification (on-device ML, no cloud needed) to identify common fungal and bacterial diseases in 3-4 major regional crops, validated against extension-service diagnoses in a single growing season pilot.

Run a field trial comparing biochar-amended vs. standard plots for water retention and yield in a drought-prone smallholder region, using cheap gravimetric soil moisture sampling rather than expensive sensors.

Build and test a $20 capacitive soil moisture sensor kit (Arduino-based) paired with SMS alerts for irrigation timing, piloted with 20 smallholder farmers to measure water savings versus current practice.

Evaluate seed priming with locally available biofertilizer strains (Rhizobium, Azospirillum) on germination rate and early vigor in legumes, using a simple randomized on-farm trial design across 10 fields.
Test whether intercropping maize with a fast-growing legume cover crop reduces need for synthetic nitrogen by 20-30% while maintaining yield, in a two-season replicated field trial.
Create a standardized, low-cost protocol using vinegar/pH strips and a simple slake test to let farmers assess soil aggregate stability and organic matter trends without lab access.
Pilot a farmer-reported pest scouting network via WhatsApp with photo submissions, aggregated weekly into a regional pest-pressure map to guide targeted spraying instead of calendar-based spraying.
Compare three plastic-mulch alternatives (straw, paper mulch, living mulch) for weed suppression and soil temperature moderation in vegetable plots, tracking cost-per-hectare and labor tradeoffs.

Design a low-cost post-harvest cold storage unit (evaporative cooling chamber) and measure shelf-life extension for leafy greens and tomatoes compared to ambient storage, with a bill of materials under $200.

Conduct a participatory on-farm variety trial letting farmers rank 5-8 candidate crop varieties for taste, yield, and resilience, feeding results back to breeding programs faster than formal multi-year trials.
Test manure composting turning frequency and windrow size effects on pathogen kill and nutrient retention, using cheap temperature loggers to optimize a protocol smallholders can replicate.
Build a simple decision-support spreadsheet/app that combines local weather forecast data with crop growth stage to recommend fungicide spray timing, reducing unnecessary applications.
Trial reduced-tillage vs. conventional tillage on a single farm cluster over two seasons, tracking soil compaction (penetrometer), yield, and fuel cost savings.
Investigate whether pre-harvest calcium chloride dips reduce post-harvest bruising and rot in apples/tomatoes during transport, using a simple drop-test and shelf storage comparison.
Develop a low-cost pheromone trap design using locally sourced materials to monitor and mass-trap key lepidopteran pests, comparing trap density needed to reduce crop damage below economic threshold.

Assess whether adding a single strain of mycorrhizal fungi inoculant to nursery transplants improves establishment and drought tolerance in field-transplanted vegetables, via a controlled nursery-to-field trial.
Quantify on-farm food loss at harvest and storage stages through simple weigh-and-log audits across a supply chain, identifying the single highest-loss node for targeted intervention.
Test small-scale solar-powered drip irrigation kits against furrow irrigation for water use efficiency and yield in a semi-arid vegetable plot, with straightforward cost-benefit analysis.
Pilot a seed-bank/seed-swap program combined with germination-rate testing kits (simple paper towel test) to help farmers avoid planting low-viability saved seed.
Study the effect of staggered planting dates (2-week intervals) on pest pressure and yield stability for a single crop, to develop simple planting-calendar recommendations for pest avoidance.
Compare three low-cost trellising/support systems for tomatoes or beans on disease incidence and yield, focusing on materials farmers can source locally.
Develop a simple color-card or app-based chlorophyll meter substitute (using phone camera calibration) to guide nitrogen top-dressing timing in cereals.
Test whether small windbreak hedgerows reduce evapotranspiration and wind erosion in open-field vegetable production, measuring soil moisture and yield gradient at increasing distance from hedgerow.
Run an on-farm comparison of vermicompost vs. conventional compost vs. synthetic fertilizer on soil microbial activity and yield in a vegetable rotation over one year.
Investigate low-cost UV-C or solar pasteurization treatment of irrigation water from contaminated sources to reduce pathogen load for leafy green production, testing pathogen counts before/after.

Pilot a simple mobile-based weather-indexed micro-insurance data collection tool tracking rainfall via cheap tipping-bucket gauges distributed to a farmer cooperative, to build a local payout trigger dataset.
Test different crop residue retention levels (0%, 30%, 60%, full) on soil moisture retention and subsequent crop establishment in a no-till system.
Evaluate feeding dairy cattle a byproduct (e.g., brewer's grain or citrus pulp) as a low-cost protein/energy supplement, measuring milk yield and feed cost changes over a controlled feeding trial.
Develop a simple field protocol combining sticky traps and degree-day tracking to predict optimal spray timing for a key regional insect pest, validated against yield loss data across multiple farms.

The Icebreaker Cards, Awkward Edition: a deck of conversation prompts engineered to produce uncomfortable silences and blunt honesty rather than smooth, forced fun. Aimed at students tired of manufactured mixer energy, it treats social discomfort as more memorable than polished small talk.

Study Timer Egg: a mechanical, non-digital kitchen egg timer repurposed for study sessions, with no app, no sync, no notifications. Its loud analog ticking enforces single-tasking by making it obvious and audible when you've stopped working, unlike a silent phone timer.

Weighted Backpack Insert: a flat insert that adds several extra pounds to any backpack, marketed as incidental strength training during the daily campus walk. It directly opposes the ultralight-gear trend, arguing that a heavier bag builds a stronger student instead of a lighter step.

The Anti-Résumé Card: a stack of business cards listing hobbies, failures, and weird trivia instead of accomplishments or GPA. Meant to be handed out ironically at career fairs, it challenges the polished-résumé culture by making failure and personality the headline instead.

Non-Rechargeable Flashlight: a cheap, single-use battery flashlight sold for dorm blackouts and camping trips, deliberately skipping rechargeable circuitry. It leans into disposability as reliability, arguing that a dead rechargeable flashlight with no outlet nearby is worse than one you simply replace.

The Quiet Party Horn: a party horn that shoots confetti and streamers but produces no sound at all. Designed for students in thin-walled dorms who want celebratory flair without a noise complaint, it separates the ritual of celebration from the volume everyone assumes it requires.

Anti-Ergo Chair Cushion: a deliberately firm, shapeless seat cushion that resists molding to your body, forcing posture shifts and shorter sitting stretches. It pushes against the ergonomic-cushion industry's promise of endless comfortable sitting, arguing mild discomfort is healthier than marathon stillness.

The Manual Sharpener Pendant: a tiny working pencil sharpener worn as a necklace, embracing analog note-taking as a fashion statement. It's aimed at students rebelling against fully digital lecture capture, making the humble pencil a visible, wearable act of resistance.

Blackout Curtain Clips: a pack of oversized binder-style clips designed to turn any spare fabric, towel, or blanket into a blackout curtain. It rejects branded dorm curtain sets entirely, betting that a cheap DIY hack beats a $40 matching curtain kit.

The Silent Roommate Bell: a small brass bell placed on a shared desk, meant to be rung instead of texting a roommate two feet away. It forces in-person, audible communication back into shared spaces where phones have quietly replaced speaking out loud.

Anti-Stress Sandpaper Cube: a rough-textured fidget cube deliberately built to feel mildly irritating rather than soothing, for students who find calm through friction instead of softness. It challenges the smooth-silicone fidget-toy market by betting that discomfort, not comfort, resets attention.

The Confidence-Killer Mirror: a small novelty mirror with a slight, humorous distortion built in, sold as an antidote to polished self-care aesthetics. It leans into imperfection and self-deprecating humor about appearance instead of the flawless-reflection promise of typical vanity mirrors.

Handwritten Letter Kit: A stationery set with pre-stamped envelopes, wax seal stamp, and blank cards, sold to encourage physical mail between friends instead of texting. Blackout Desk Tent: A collapsible fabric hood that clips over a dorm desk, blocking all ambient light and roommate distraction, turning any desk into a sensory-deprivation study booth. It opposes the open, bright, Instagrammable study space trend by embracing a dark, cave-like alternative.

Manual Coffee Grinder Only: A hand-crank burr grinder sold without any electric counterpart offered, betting students will accept five extra minutes for better coffee and a screen-free morning ritual. It opposes the pod-machine convenience trend that dominates dorm kitchens.

Wired-Only Earbuds: A basic pair of corded earbuds with no Bluetooth, batteries, or charging case, sold at a fraction of wireless earbud prices. It opposes the assumption that wireless is strictly an upgrade, betting on reliability, zero-charging-anxiety, and durability against dorm-room loss.

No-Group-Chat Bulletin Board: A small corkboard and pushpin set marketed for coordinating roommate chores and messages physically instead of via group text, sold as 'the original notifications-free app.' It bets shared physical space communication reduces group-chat overload and passive-aggressive texting.

candidates.text: Instead of asking which features to cut, cut the roadmap review meeting itself — let the release ship with whatever survives benign neglect, since nobody actually agreed on the criteria anyway.

Rank features by how painful it would be to lose political face, then deliberately cut the one the loudest executive champions — if it can't survive without their sponsorship, it was never product-market fit, just power fit.
Cut the most-loved feature, not the least-used one: high affection often masks a vocal minority propping up something that quietly costs the majority speed and clarity.
Instead of usage data, use a willingness-to-pay test: tell users a feature will become a $2/month add-on and cut anything nobody opts into, revealing real value versus assumed value.
Freeze the team in a room without their dashboards or telemetry and ask them to rebuild the product from memory in a day; whatever they forget to include is what gets cut.
Give the cutting decision to the newest hires, who have no sunk-cost attachment and no memory of why anything was built, rather than to the founders who built it.
Institute a strict '2-for-1' rule: nothing new ships unless two existing things are removed first, forcing scarcity thinking retroactively across the whole backlog, not just this release.

Ignore usage metrics entirely and cut based on maintenance cost per engineer-hour — the feature draining the most invisible debugging time each sprint goes, regardless of how beloved or visible it is.
Run a 30-day 'silent removal' experiment: quietly disable a feature with no announcement and see if anyone notices or complains before deciding for real — silence is truer signal than surveys.
Ask sales and support what they are embarrassed to demo or explain to a new customer; cut whatever makes your own team wince, since internal shame is a leading indicator no dashboard shows.

Reverse the survivorship bias: instead of cutting what's unused, cut what's used constantly as a workaround — heavy usage of a clunky feature often signals a broken core experience being patched over, not value.
Let customers vote publicly on what to cut, but weight votes inversely to how much they actually use the product — infrequent users see clutter the power users have become blind to.
Cut nothing in the product and instead cut the release cycle itself — ship less often, and let the absence of a deadline reveal which 'urgent' features were actually manufactured urgency.

Audit every feature flag that's been 'temporarily' left on for over a year; the temporary-permanent ones are prime candidates, since nobody had the courage to make the permanent decision the first time.
Have engineering estimate what it would cost to rebuild each feature from scratch today with current knowledge; cut anything nobody would choose to build again, regardless of past investment.

Cut whichever feature has the most internal documentation and onboarding material — the amount of institutional hand-holding required is itself evidence the feature is too confusing to justify existing.
Instead of trusting the product team's judgment, outsource the cutting decision to an external red-team who has never used the product, asking them to identify what feels bloated on first contact.
Run an internal prediction market where employees bet real stakes on which features will be missed after removal; trust the market price over any stakeholder's stated opinion.
Assume every complaint about removing a feature is evidence it should stay off longer, not shorter — treat backlash as confirmation of dependency, which is precisely the coupling worth breaking.
Cut based on emotional sunk cost directly: identify the feature the founding team is proudest of and specifically interrogate whether that pride, not user need, is what's kept it alive this long.
Instead of cutting product features, cut the metrics and KPIs currently used to justify keeping features — if the measurement framework itself is broken, no feature audit built on it can be trusted.

Ask what a scrappy two-person competitor would ship if forced to rebuild your product in a week; anything they'd obviously omit is your cut list, because complexity accretes invisibly inside incumbents.

Cut the feature most often cited in investor pitches or marketing decks — if it exists mainly to sound impressive externally rather than serve users internally, its purpose was narrative, not function.
Impose a mandatory cooling-off period: nothing gets cut until it's been formally 'sentenced' but kept dormant for one release cycle, forcing the team to prove they miss it before removal is final.
Deputize customer support tickets as the sole cutting criterion, but invert the usual logic — cut features generating zero tickets, since zero friction can mean zero engagement, not perfection.

Assign a randomized 'sacrifice lottery' among mid-tier features: pick one truly at random to remove each release regardless of data, forcing the org to build resilience instead of feature-hoarding habits.

Cut whatever was built to satisfy a single enterprise customer's one-time request, even if that customer is still paying — bespoke debt disguised as a feature quietly taxes every other user's experience.
Reject usage data as a cutting signal altogether and instead interview the engineers who maintain each feature, asking which one they'd quit over having to support for another year.
Cut the onboarding flow's most 'essential' step first, on the theory that anything defended as non-negotiable during a cutting exercise is exactly the assumption most overdue for testing.

Instead of deciding centrally, let each team member secretly nominate one feature to kill anonymously; publish the tally and force public defense only for items nominated by more than one person, removing groupthink protection for pet projects.

candidates.text: Single flat-rate plan: one price, full feature set, no tiers to simplify decision-making and messaging at launch.

Freemium model with a capped free tier that drives adoption and virality, converting a percentage of users to paid once they hit usage or feature limits.
Usage-based metered pricing where customers pay per unit consumed (API calls, minutes, transactions), aligning cost directly with value received.

Value-based pricing set according to the measurable ROI or outcome the product delivers to the customer, rather than cost or competitor price.
Cost-plus pricing: calculate total cost to serve (infra, support, dev) and add a target margin to set the subscription price.
Competitive benchmarking pricing that positions the product slightly above, at, or below known competitor price points to signal quality or value.
Penetration pricing: launch at an artificially low price to rapidly capture market share, then raise prices once a user base and switching costs are established.
Price skimming: launch at a premium price targeting early adopters willing to pay for novelty, then progressively lower prices as the market matures.
Dynamic/real-time pricing that adjusts based on demand, time of day, capacity, or individual usage patterns, similar to ride-share or airline pricing.
Pay-what-you-want pricing with a suggested minimum, relying on trust and goodwill while still capturing higher-paying customers voluntarily.
Lifetime founding-member deal: a one-time upfront payment grants permanent access, generating early cash flow and rewarding first adopters.
Annual vs. monthly billing options with a meaningful discount for annual prepayment to improve cash flow and reduce churn.
Hybrid base-fee-plus-overage model: a low fixed subscription covers a usage allotment, with metered charges kicking in beyond that threshold.
Bundling the subscription with a complementary product or service (e.g., hardware, another SaaS tool) to increase perceived value and differentiate from single-product competitors.
Geographic/purchasing-power-parity pricing that adjusts subscription cost by region to match local income levels and maximize global reach.

Reverse trial: give new users full premium access for a limited period, then automatically downgrade them to a restricted free tier unless they subscribe.

Unlimited all-inclusive flat fee with no tiers or usage caps, marketed on simplicity and predictability of cost.
Decoy-tier anchoring: introduce a deliberately less attractive middle tier to make the premium tier look like the obviously better deal by comparison.

Token or credit-based system where subscribers buy a pool of credits redeemable across any feature or service, offering flexibility over rigid tiers.

Run cohort-based A/B pricing experiments at launch, offering different price points to different user segments to empirically determine willingness to pay.
Outcome/performance-based pricing where customers pay a fee only when the product delivers a specific measurable result, shifting risk to the provider.

Native XLSX export that preserves cell formatting, formulas, and multiple sheets rather than flattening everything to plain text.
Direct push integration to Google Sheets, writing data into a live spreadsheet the user selects, with optional auto-refresh.
Scheduled recurring exports (daily/weekly/monthly) automatically delivered to email or a cloud storage destination.
OAuth-based export to third-party cloud storage (Dropbox, S3, OneDrive) so files land directly in the user's own storage account.
A public/authenticated REST API endpoint that returns data in JSON/CSV, letting developers build custom export pipelines.
A GraphQL export interface where users can construct arbitrary queries to shape exactly which fields and relations get exported.

A shareable read-only export link that renders a snapshot of data as a hosted web page, viewable without downloading a file.
Copy-to-clipboard quick export that formats selected data as Markdown or plain text for pasting into docs/chat.
Export as structured code/config (JSON, YAML, or a code snippet) tailored for developers integrating with the product.
Row/record-level selective export via checkboxes, letting users cherry-pick exactly which items to include.
Full SQL database dump option for self-hosted customers who want to migrate or back up their entire dataset.
Print-optimized export that generates a clean, paginated PDF layout suitable for physical printing.

Chart/visualization export as static image files (PNG/SVG) for embedding in presentations or documents.
Export to presentation format (PowerPoint/Keynote slides) auto-populated with key charts and summary tables.
Command-line interface (CLI) tool that power users can script to pull and export data on demand.
Browser extension that captures the current in-app session state and exports it locally without needing server-side support.
