candidates.text: Usage telemetry threshold: cut any feature below a defined minimum active-usage percentage over the last quarter.
Cost-of-ownership audit: calculate engineering and support hours consumed per feature per month and cut those costing more than they return in value.
Zero-based feature budgeting: require every existing feature to be re-justified from scratch as if it were a brand-new proposal, and cut anything that fails to win approval.
Pre-committed kill criteria: for every feature shipped, define in advance the conditions under which it would be sunset, then apply those triggers now instead of waiting.
Reverse stack-ranking: force-rank all current features and screens from most to least valuable, then cut the bottom 10-20% regardless of sentiment.
Support ticket cost analysis: identify features generating the highest ratio of support tickets to active users and remove the worst offenders first.
Silent deprecation test: hide a feature behind a flag for a subset of users and observe whether anyone notices or complains before making removal permanent.
Direct customer survey: ask active users which features they would be fine losing, and cut based on the most consistent low-attachment responses.
Strategic alignment scoring: score every feature against the current one-sentence product strategy and cut anything that doesn't visibly serve it.
Complexity-vs-value matrix: plot features by engineering complexity against measured user value, then cut everything in the high-complexity/low-value quadrant.
Revenue attribution model: trace which features correlate with retained paying customers versus which are pure cost centers, and cut the latter.
Documentation and tribal-knowledge audit: flag any feature no one on the team can clearly explain or find documented, treating it as a default cut candidate.
Leadership vision test: have leaders imagine pitching the product from scratch and cut anything they wouldn't naturally include in that pitch.
Age-based sunset rule: automatically flag any feature untouched by users and engineers for more than a set number of months as a removal candidate.
Cross-functional cut committee: assemble a rotating panel from support, sales, engineering, and design to jointly nominate and vote on removals separately from the roadmap team.
A/B removal experiment: disable a feature for a random cohort and measure churn or engagement impact before deciding permanently.
Interdependency mapping: identify features with no downstream dependencies as lower-risk, easier candidates for removal.
Segment overlap analysis: cut features that serve only a small, already-served-elsewhere customer segment, especially if it isn't strategically important.
Outside-in advisory review: bring in customers or advisors unfamiliar with internal politics to give a blunt read on what looks unnecessary.
Compliance and risk-driven removal: identify features carrying disproportionate legal, security, or compliance risk relative to their benefit and cut those first.
One-job focus method: define the single job the product must do best, and cut anything that doesn't directly support that job.
Diminishing-returns comparison: for near-duplicate features or variants, compare their performance and keep only the highest-performing version.
Deprecation announcement with opt-out tracking: publicly announce a planned removal and weight the final decision by how much real pushback actually occurs.
Internal dogfooding vote: ask employees who use the product daily to flag features they personally avoid, treating consistent avoidance as a cut signal.
Chaos-removal drill: randomly disable several features in a staging or beta environment and see which absences actually get noticed or reported by testers.
Cost-per-maintained-code audit: correlate lines of code or infrastructure spend per feature against usage data to flag expensive-to-maintain, low-usage code.
Competitive necessity check: compare each feature against market table-stakes and cut anything that is neither differentiating nor expected by the market.
Time-to-value regression test: identify features that slow onboarding or delay first value without proportionate benefit, and cut those first.
Capacity-constraint simulation: imagine the team has only 70% of current time or headcount for the release and derive a cut list from what couldn't survive that reduction.
Emotional attachment audit: identify features being kept mainly due to sentiment or sunk-cost bias, and require a fresh business justification within a deadline or cut them.

candidates.text: Instrument every feature with usage analytics and cut anything below a defined engagement threshold (e.g., used by <2% of active users in the last 90 days).
Run a 'silent kill switch' test: disable a feature flag for a subset of users without announcement and see if anyone notices or complains before deciding to remove it permanently.
Build a cost-to-maintain ledger (engineering hours, cloud spend, support tickets) per feature and cut whichever have the worst maintenance-cost-to-value ratio.
Ask support and success teams to rank features by support ticket volume relative to adoption, and remove the ones generating disproportionate friction for few users.
Hold a pre-mortem: imagine the release failed and work backward to identify which features most likely caused complexity, delay, or confusion, then cut those first.
Map every feature to current OKRs/strategic pillars; anything that doesn't trace to an active company priority becomes a cut candidate.
Do a technical debt and complexity audit, ranking features by how much architectural entanglement or fragility they introduce, and remove the worst offenders.
Survey or interview customers directly with the question 'what would you not miss if it disappeared tomorrow?' and use the aggregated answers as a cut list.
Apply zero-based budgeting to the feature set: require every feature to be re-justified from scratch as if proposing it new, and cut anything that can't earn its place.
Analyze session recordings/heatmaps for signs of confusion, abandonment, or unused UI elements, and remove features associated with poor interaction patterns.
Set predefined 'sunset criteria' at each feature's original launch (e.g., must hit X adoption by Y date) and mechanically cut anything that fails to meet its own bar.
Have engineers anonymously vote on the features they most dread maintaining or debugging, and prioritize those for removal regardless of usage stats.
Run an A/B test removing a feature for a subset of users and measure churn, satisfaction, or revenue impact before committing to a permanent cut.
Benchmark against competitors and industry leaders to find commoditized or expected-but-non-differentiating features, then cut what no longer sets the product apart.
Perform a revenue attribution analysis linking features to actual paying-customer retention or upgrade behavior, cutting those with no measurable financial tie.
Conduct a security and compliance risk audit, and remove features whose risk exposure (data handling, legacy protocols, unpatched dependencies) outweighs their benefit.
Use a dependency graph of the codebase to identify 'leaf' features with minimal downstream reliance, making them safer, lower-risk cut candidates.
Convene an executive gut-check session where leadership reviews the full feature list and makes subjective brand/strategy-fit judgments on what to cut.
Analyze data staleness: identify features whose underlying data hasn't been updated, queried, or acted upon in a long time, signaling abandonment.
Time-box a 'removal sprint' where the team can cut anything untouched by users or code changes in the last N months, no further justification required.
Map the primary user journey and audit cognitive load; cut secondary features that clutter or slow down the critical path, even if occasionally used.
Poll or mine sentiment from community forums, app store reviews, and social media to identify features users complain about or explicitly wish were gone.
Segment customers by value tier and check feature usage per segment; cut features that serve only low-value or churned segments.
Estimate the release-time cost of keeping each feature (QA cycles, regression risk, documentation updates) and cut whichever most delays or destabilizes the release.
Apply a RICE-style scoring model in reverse (lowest reach, impact, confidence per effort) to rank and cut the weakest-scoring existing features.
Assemble an external advisory panel or customer council to independently review and vote on which features add the least value to their workflows.
Audit documentation and onboarding materials for features that require disproportionate explanation relative to their use, treating explanatory burden as a red flag.
Trace each feature's origin story (why it was built, for whom) and cut ones whose original justification no longer holds or whose sponsor/champion has left.
Use a 'cost of choice' UX principle: for every optional setting or toggle, ask if removing it would meaningfully harm any user, and eliminate ones that mostly add decision fatigue.
Run a legal/regulatory review to identify features creating ongoing compliance overhead or liability, and cut those where the regulatory cost has grown to outweigh their value.
